did_you_know.text: Ecclesiastes begins by examining joy and goodness, but at the very start of this search he concludes that they too are meaningless.
Ecclesiastes describes a combined experiment: he turns to wine and bodily pleasures, while continuing to act wisely in order to discover what is good for people during their lives.
As part of his experiment, Ecclesiastes describes building and planting projects: he builds houses and plants vineyards.
Ecclesiastes makes pools of water to irrigate a forest growing trees, describing a planned use of resources for his projects.
Ecclesiastes lists among his possessions silver, gold, the treasures of kings and provinces, as well as music and human pleasures.
Ecclesiastes says that he denied his eyes nothing they desired, and that his joy in his work was the reward he received from all his labor.
After reflecting on all he had done and all his labor, Ecclesiastes concludes that everything is meaningless and chasing the wind, and that nothing is gained under the sun.
Ecclesiastes recognizes that wisdom is better than foolishness, just as light is better than darkness.
The wise person is described as having eyes in his head, while the fool walks in darkness. Nevertheless, Ecclesiastes notes that the same fate will overtake them both.
Ecclesiastes presents eating, drinking, and enjoying the fruits of one’s labor as possible good for a person, adding that this too is a gift from God.
